<!-- https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v0.5.0/giong-mcp/README.md -->

# giong-mcp

An [MCP](https://modelcontextprotocol.io) server that lets an AI agent look inside a running [giong](https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v0.5.0/README.md) service: what each worker is doing, which tasks are alive and which line spawned them, what the connection pools hold, and where the time goes. Read-only, on a loopback address or a Unix socket, and only when the service turns it on.

```toml
[dependencies]
giong = "0.5"
giong-mcp = "0.5"
```

```rust
fn main() -> std::io::Result<()> {
    let rt = giong::Builder::new().shutdown_on_signals(true).build()?;
    // Starts only when GIONG_MCP is set, for example GIONG_MCP=127.0.0.1:7777.
    let _mcp = giong_mcp::start_from_env(&rt.handle())?;
    rt.run(|_worker| async {
        // ... the service ...
        giong::shutdown_signal().await;
    })
}
```

```sh
GIONG_MCP=127.0.0.1:7777 cargo run --release
claude mcp add --transport http giong http://127.0.0.1:7777/mcp    # Claude Code
```

Any MCP client that speaks the Streamable HTTP transport works the same way. In code, `giong_mcp::Config::tcp("127.0.0.1:7777").token(secret).start(&handle)` does the same as the environment variables, and `Config::unix(path)` listens on a Unix socket.

## What an agent can ask

| Tool | Answers |
|---|---|
| `overview` | The process (resident memory, threads, open descriptors against the limit, uptime), the runtime (workers, shutdown, profiling), each worker's state, I/O driver, live tasks, busy share and polls per second over the last second, and warnings. |
| `workers` | Each worker in detail: counters since start (event-loop turns, polls, sleeps, idle time, spawned tasks), rates over the last second, timers, I/O operations in flight, receive buffers, draining, and the task a blocked worker is stuck in. |
| `tasks` | Live tasks grouped by the line that spawned them, across workers or for one (`worker`, `limit`). A count that keeps growing at one line is a leak. |
| `sources` | What registered sources report, summed over workers and per worker: giong-postgres, giong-mysql and giong-redis pools (open, taken, connecting, in flight, waiting, opened, connect errors, timeouts) and anything registered with `giong::observe::register`. |
| `profile` | Times every task poll for `duration_ms` (100 to 10,000, default 1,000), then lists the spawn locations the workers spent their time in: polls, total, share of the window, mean and longest poll. |

The answer that matters most is the one other tools cannot give: **which task blocks a worker.** giong runs many tasks on one thread, so a task that calls a blocking function or computes for a long time without `.await` stalls every other task on its worker. The server samples each worker ten times a second; a worker that is awake but has not moved on is reported with the spawn location of the task it is in:

```json
"warnings": [
  "worker 1 has been inside one poll of the task spawned at src/routes/report.rs:88:13 for 2.3 s: that task blocks the thread (a blocking call, a long computation or a loop without .await), and every other task on worker 1 waits"
]
```

The server runs on a thread and a single-worker giong runtime of its own, so it answers even when every worker of the service is stuck. A worker that cannot answer within `snapshot_timeout` (500 ms by default) is reported as such, with what its counters say.

## How it works

The runtime keeps the data; this crate only serves it. In `giong`:

- Every worker publishes counters and the spawn location of the task it is polling, on a cache line of its own, with relaxed stores: `Handle::pulse(worker)` reads them from any thread without disturbing the worker. That costs about nine instructions per task poll (two of them stores; counted with callgrind on tasks that only yield) and one store per turn of the event loop.
- `spawn`, `Handle::spawn_on` and `Handle::spawn_balanced` record where they were called (`#[track_caller]`), so a task is named by a line of your code, and `observe::snapshot()` groups the live tasks by it.
- `Handle::set_profiling(true)` makes every worker read the clock around each poll; when it is off, it costs one relaxed load per batch of tasks (the loop is compiled twice, with and without the clock).
- Pools register themselves as `observe::Source`s, by weak reference.

## Security

Whoever can reach the server can read the internals of the service: task locations, pool addresses (never user names or passwords), memory figures. So:

- It listens on `127.0.0.1`, `::1` or a Unix socket, and refuses any other address with [GIONG-E1301](https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v0.5.0/docs/errors/E1301.md). To reach a service elsewhere, forward the port (`ssh -L 7777:127.0.0.1:7777 host`, `kubectl port-forward`).
- A request whose `Host` header is not a loopback name, or whose `Origin` is not a loopback origin, is refused with `403`: a web page cannot reach the server through DNS rebinding.
- With a token (`GIONG_MCP_TOKEN`, `Config::token`), every request needs `Authorization: Bearer <token>`; without one, any local process that can connect can read.
- Every tool is read-only. Nothing can change the service through it, apart from `profile` turning poll timing on for the time it measures.

## Protocol

MCP over Streamable HTTP at `/mcp`, protocol versions 2025-11-25, 2025-06-18 and 2025-03-26. One JSON-RPC message (or a batch) per `POST`, answered with `application/json`; notifications get `202 Accepted`. The server offers no event stream (`GET` gets `405`) and keeps no sessions. Tool results carry the JSON both as `structuredContent` and as text.

## Testing

`cargo test -p giong-mcp`: 16 tests. Seven run a two-worker service with a server on a loopback port and a plain HTTP client: the handshake and tool list, every tool's answer checked against known tasks and sources, a worker blocked in `std::thread::sleep` reported with its line while the other worker still answers, a profile finding a busy task, JSON-RPC errors, and the refusals (token, `Host`, `Origin`, method, content type, protocol version, non-loopback addresses, a Unix socket that replaces a stale one). Eight unit tests cover address parsing, the `Host` check, version negotiation, the watcher, `/proc` and a `profile` call dropped half-way (profiling goes back off), and one the documentation example. `tests/observe.rs` in the runtime (8 tests) checks the counters, spawn locations, profiles and sources underneath, on both drivers.

## License

MIT or Apache-2.0, at your option.

<!-- https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v0.5.0/giong-compat/README.md -->

# giong-compat

The I/O traits of Tokio and of the futures crates for [giong](https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v0.5.0/README.md)'s streams, so that protocol crates which are generic over their transport run on giong: TLS (tokio-rustls, futures-rustls), WebSocket (tokio-tungstenite), HTTP/2 (h2), hyper's connection API, framing (tokio-util's codecs) and the like. No Tokio runtime is involved: giong drives everything, on its own threads.

```toml
[dependencies]
giong = "0.5"
giong-compat = "0.5"
```

```rust
use giong::net::TcpStream;
use giong_compat::Compat;
use tokio::io::{AsyncReadExt, AsyncWriteExt};

fn main() -> std::io::Result<()> {
    giong::block_on(async {
        let mut stream = Compat::new(TcpStream::connect("127.0.0.1:7000").await?);
        stream.write_all(b"ping\n").await?;
        stream.flush().await?; // writes are buffered until a flush, or until a read waits
        let mut reply = [0; 5];
        stream.read_exact(&mut reply).await?;
        Ok(())
    })
}
```

`Compat<S>` wraps a `giong::net::TcpStream`, a `giong::net::UnixStream` or, with the `tls` feature, a `giong_tls::TlsStream`, and implements `AsyncRead`, `AsyncWrite` and `AsyncBufRead` from `tokio::io` (feature `tokio`) and from `futures_io` (feature `futures-io`). Both features are on by default and pull in the trait definitions only: `tokio` with its default features off, so no runtime, reactor or timer. The libraries build on Rust 1.80.

## When to use it, and when not

Use the native crate when there is one. It is built on giong's owned buffers and batched system calls, and is faster than the same protocol through this adapter.

| You need | Use |
|---|---|
| An HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2 server or client | [`giong-http`](https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v0.5.0/giong-http/README.md); [`giong-web`](https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v0.5.0/giong-web/README.md) for routing and JSON |
| TLS | [`giong-tls`](https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v0.5.0/giong-tls/README.md) |
| PostgreSQL, MySQL, Redis | [`giong-postgres`](https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v0.5.0/giong-postgres/README.md), [`giong-mysql`](https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v0.5.0/giong-mysql/README.md), [`giong-redis`](https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v0.5.0/giong-redis/README.md) |
| h2's own API (HTTP/2 frames and streams, or a library built on h2) | [h2](https://docs.rs/h2) over `Compat`, plain or over `giong-tls` with ALPN `h2` |
| WebSocket | [tokio-tungstenite](https://docs.rs/tokio-tungstenite) (`accept_async`, `client_async`) over `Compat` |
| A protocol framed by length or by line | [tokio-util](https://docs.rs/tokio-util)'s `Framed` with a codec over `Compat` |
| hyper's API in particular | `hyper::{client, server}::conn` over `hyper_util::rt::TokioIo::new(Compat::new(..))`; a server needs a timer, [see below](#hyper-servers-need-a-timer) |
| A crate that opens its own connections with Tokio (reqwest, tonic's `transport`, sqlx, most SDKs) | Not `Compat`: see below |

### What works

A crate works through `Compat` when **it takes the stream from you and you drive it**: a function such as `tokio_rustls::TlsConnector::connect(name, stream)`, `tokio_tungstenite::client_async(request, stream)`, `h2::client::handshake(stream)` or `hyper::client::conn::http1::handshake(io)`, which returns a future, or a connection object, that your task (or a task you start with `giong::spawn`) polls. Futures that are not `Send` are fine, since giong's tasks stay on their worker.

These are tested in [`tests/`](https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v0.5.0/giong-compat/tests), on giong's io_uring driver, its older ring setups and its epoll driver, with no Tokio runtime in the process:

| Crate | What the tests do |
|---|---|
| tokio-rustls 0.26 | A tokio-rustls client against a giong-tls server, and a giong-tls client against a tokio-rustls server (ALPN, `close_notify`), up to 1 MiB per message |
| futures-rustls 0.26 | A futures-rustls client (futures-io traits) against a giong-tls server |
| tokio-tungstenite 0.29 | A WebSocket echo server and client: text, a 4 MiB binary message, 1,000 messages queued before any is read, ping and pong, the close handshake |
| h2 0.4 | An HTTP/2 server and client: 100 streams at once on one connection with bodies over several flow-control windows; and h2 over giong-tls with ALPN `h2` |
| hyper 1 (HTTP/1) | hyper's client against a giong-http server, and giong-http's client against a hyper server, with keep-alive and bodies up to 500 KB; a hyper server with a timer on giong's timers closes a connection whose request head does not arrive in time |
| tokio-util 0.7 | `LengthDelimitedCodec` over a Unix socket (200 frames up to 1 MB) and `LinesCodec` over TCP |

### What does not

`Compat` provides I/O traits, nothing else. A crate does not work through it when it

- **opens its own connections with `tokio::net`** (reqwest, tonic's `transport`, sqlx, redis-rs, most cloud SDKs): it panics with *"there is no reactor running, must be called from the context of a Tokio 1.x runtime"*, or never finishes;
- **uses Tokio's timers or spawns** (`tokio::time::sleep`, `tokio::time::timeout`, `tokio::spawn`): the same panic. hyper takes its timer and executor from you instead: see [hyper servers need a timer](#hyper-servers-need-a-timer);
- **requires `Send`** (bounds such as `T: Send` or `F: Future + Send + 'static`): `Compat` is not `Send`, because the stream belongs to one worker. The compiler says so.

Some of these crates take a custom connector or executor, and can work with one built on giong, but each has to be tried. Otherwise, run the crate on a Tokio runtime in a thread of its own.

### hyper servers need a timer

hyper's server enforces no timeout of its own: `header_read_timeout` needs a `hyper::rt::Timer`, and without one a client that sends half a request head and then nothing holds the connection, and the task serving it, for as long as it likes. Setting the timeout without a timer panics. giong's timers can back one:

```rust
use std::pin::Pin;
use std::task::{Context, Poll};
use std::time::{Duration, Instant};

/// hyper's timer, on giong's timers.
#[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug)]
struct GiongTimer;

struct GiongSleep(giong::time::Sleep);

impl std::future::Future for GiongSleep {
    type Output = ();
    fn poll(mut self: Pin<&mut Self>, cx: &mut Context<'_>) -> Poll<()> {
        Pin::new(&mut self.0).poll(cx)
    }
}

impl hyper::rt::Sleep for GiongSleep {}

impl hyper::rt::Timer for GiongTimer {
    fn sleep(&self, duration: Duration) -> Pin<Box<dyn hyper::rt::Sleep>> {
        Box::pin(GiongSleep(giong::time::sleep(duration)))
    }
    fn sleep_until(&self, deadline: Instant) -> Pin<Box<dyn hyper::rt::Sleep>> {
        Box::pin(GiongSleep(giong::time::sleep_until(deadline)))
    }
}

// For each accepted connection:
// hyper::server::conn::http1::Builder::new()
//     .timer(GiongTimer)
//     .header_read_timeout(Duration::from_secs(10))
//     .serve_connection(hyper_util::rt::TokioIo::new(Compat::new(tcp)), service)
```

[`tests/hyper.rs`](https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v0.5.0/giong-compat/tests/hyper.rs) checks that a server built this way closes such a connection when the timeout ends.

## How it behaves

- **Writes are buffered**, as with `BufWriter` or a TLS stream. `poll_write` copies the bytes and returns; they are sent on `flush`, when the buffer is full, or when a read on the same task is about to wait. Call `flush` (or `shutdown`) where the data must have gone out; every crate written for these traits does. A writer in another task than the reader must flush: a read only sends what its own task wrote. While one buffer is being sent the next one fills, so a long transfer keeps the socket busy.
- **The write buffer is bounded**: `Compat::new(stream).write_buffer(limit)`, 64 KiB by default, from 1 byte to 1 GiB (`GIONG-E1403` otherwise). A busy stream holds up to twice the limit. An idle one may keep one empty buffer of up to the limit after a burst of writes (on the io_uring driver, where a send can still be running when the next write comes); for many mostly idle connections, give them a smaller limit.
- **`TCP_NODELAY` is turned on** for TCP streams (plain or under TLS), as every giong crate does. `Compat` already gathers small writes until a flush, and Nagle's algorithm on top of that only delays them: the HTTP/2 test with 100 streams took 2.3 s with it and 21 ms without. `compat.get_ref().set_nodelay(false)` undoes it.
- **A failed send is reported by the next write, flush or shutdown**, with the kernel's own error; after that, writes, flushes and shutdowns fail with `GIONG-E1401`. Writing after `shutdown` (or `close`) fails with `GIONG-E1402`. Reading still works in both cases. A shutdown that finds the connection already reset counts as done, as with Tokio's `TcpStream`.
- **Dropping a `Compat` discards what was written but not flushed**, like dropping a `BufWriter`. Sends in flight are cancelled the way giong cancels any operation: their buffers stay alive until the kernel lets go.
- **One task reads and one task writes at a time.** `tokio::io::split` and `futures::io::AsyncReadExt::split` work, and so does splitting a `Framed` or a WebSocket stream.
- **Cancel safe.** A read that is dropped loses no data. A write either copies bytes and says how many, or copies nothing.
- **Reading after the end of the stream** keeps returning 0 bytes. `into_inner().await` flushes and hands back the stream with the bytes received but not yet read, to go on with giong's own API.

## What it costs

giong reads into buffers from the worker's pool and writes buffers it owns until the kernel is done with them; these traits read into, and write from, memory the caller lends for one call. So `Compat` copies:

- **Reading:** each byte once more than giong's own `recv`, from the pool buffer into the caller's buffer. Through `AsyncBufRead` (`fill_buf`, then `consume` of the whole chunk) there is no extra copy. When a caller takes only part of a chunk, the rest moves to a heap buffer at once, so that a slow reader never holds on to the worker's pool.
- **Writing:** each byte once, into the write buffer, which giong's `write_all` then sends. One small allocation per send (the future that sends it).

Measured with [`bench/compat.sh`](https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v0.5.0/bench/compat.sh): one TCP stream over loopback, the measured side on one pinned core and the other end on another, the same peer for every variant, 9 runs interleaved. Median, with the range of the 9 runs in brackets. The machine is a 4-vCPU cloud VM (Xeon at 2.1 GHz, Linux 6.18), where bulk transfers over loopback vary from run to run and from one session to the next: read the medians, the spread, and the four sessions below. This session ran on `main` at `8632eb7`.

| Workload | giong's own API | `Compat` | `Compat`, `AsyncBufRead` | Tokio |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Receive 2 GiB (peer writes 256 KiB at a time), MiB/s | 3025 [2716–3134] | 2943 [2628–3550] | 3042 [2881–3247] | 2932 [2788–3519] |
| CPU per KiB received | 159 ns | 180 ns | 152 ns | 131 ns |
| Send 2 GiB from a 64 KiB buffer, MiB/s | 2475 [2042–2728] | 2220 [1918–2442] | | 2389 [1915–3312] |
| CPU per KiB sent | 382 ns | 437 ns | | 408 ns |
| 64-byte request and reply, round trips/s | 29,939 [26,924–32,057] | 29,368 [27,930–32,680] | | 31,572 [29,479–33,692] |
| CPU per round trip | 15.7 µs | 15.9 µs | | 14.9 µs |

CPU is the measured thread's own (user and system, `CLOCK_THREAD_CPUTIME_ID`).

The cost of `Compat` moves from one session of 9 runs to the next by more than the difference it measures. Four sessions on the same machine type, each the medians of 9 runs, `Compat` against giong's own API:

| Session (commit) | Send, MiB/s | Send, CPU per KiB | Receive with `read`, CPU per KiB | Receive with `AsyncBufRead`, CPU per KiB | Request and reply, round trips/s | CPU per round trip |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 (`f992163`) | −12.5% | +13.8% | +5.8% | −2.2% | −2.8% | +4.7% |
| 2 (`0bd788a`) | −16.1% | +19.4% | +11.8% | +3.9% | +1.2% | +3.4% |
| 3 (`0bd788a`) | −20.1% | +25.1% | +13.2% | +8.7% | −0.7% | +3.5% |
| 4 (`8632eb7`, the table above) | −10.3% | +14.6% | +13.1% | −4.6% | −1.9% | +1.4% |

What the numbers say:

- **Sending** through `Compat` gives up 10–20% of throughput and spends 14–25% more CPU per byte than passing an owned buffer to giong's `write_all`. That is the copy: under callgrind, `memcpy` is 96% of the user-space instructions `Compat` runs on this workload. Tokio, which writes straight from the caller's memory, is within 6% of giong's throughput in every session.
- **Receiving** through `read` costs 6–13% more CPU per byte than giong's own `recv`, for the copy into the caller's buffer, at the same throughput. Through `AsyncBufRead` (`fill_buf`, then `consume`) there is no copy: the four sessions put it between 5% below and 9% above giong's own cost, which is the noise between sessions.
- **Request and reply** differ by less than the noise in throughput; the CPU per round trip is 1–5% higher. Callgrind counts about 1,000 more user-space instructions per round trip (the boxed send, the flush, one more poll), against roughly 16 µs spent mostly in the kernel.
- **Tokio's own receive spends less CPU per KiB** than giong's `recv` on this benchmark, 6–18% less across the sessions. That gap is giong's own, not `Compat`'s.

Run it with `bench/compat.sh` (the method is at the top of the script, and in [`bench/compat/src/main.rs`](https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v0.5.0/bench/compat/src/main.rs)); the raw numbers of the latest session are in [`bench/results/compat/`](https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v0.5.0/bench/results/compat), the earlier ones in its `sessions/` folder.

## Errors

| Code | When |
|---|---|
| [`GIONG-E1401`](https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v0.5.0/docs/errors/E1401.md) | A write, flush or shutdown after a buffered send failed (the first call after the failure got the kernel's error) |
| [`GIONG-E1402`](https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v0.5.0/docs/errors/E1402.md) | A write after `shutdown` or `close` |
| [`GIONG-E1403`](https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v0.5.0/docs/errors/E1403.md) | `write_buffer` given 0 or more than 1 GiB (a panic) |

`giong::error::code(&err)` returns the code, to match on instead of the message.

<!-- https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v0.5.0/docs/DEPLOYMENT.md -->

# Deploying giong

giong is fastest on io_uring, which needs Linux 6.0 or newer (6.1 or newer recommended)
and the three io_uring system calls: `io_uring_setup`, `io_uring_enter` and
`io_uring_register`. Many container platforms block them by default.

Where io_uring cannot be used, giong runs on its **epoll driver** instead, without being
told: in a Docker container with the default seccomp profile, in Kubernetes with the
`RuntimeDefault` profile, under gVisor, with the `kernel.io_uring_disabled` sysctl set,
on a kernel older than 6.0, or on Linux 6.14 to 7.2 when the
[locked-memory limit](#locked-memory-limit) is used up. Every API works the same way on
both drivers; epoll makes more system calls per request, and file operations run on a
pool of blocking threads.
When giong falls back by itself it says so once on stderr, with the reason (the same
`GIONG-E…` error a runtime that insists on io_uring would get). `giong::driver_choice()`
tells which driver a worker got, who chose it, and why io_uring is not used; log it at
startup:

```rust
giong::block_on(async {
    eprintln!("giong driver: {}", giong::driver_choice());
    // io_uring (chosen automatically)
});
```

`giong-mcp`'s `overview` shows the same for each worker. The
[README](https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v0.5.0/README.md#two-drivers-io_uring-and-epoll) has the measured difference.

So a container needs no special settings to run giong. Allow io_uring, as this page shows,
when you want its speed:

- `Builder::driver(DriverKind::IoUring)`, or `GIONG_DRIVER=io_uring` in the environment,
  makes the runtime fail to start where io_uring is blocked, instead of running on epoll.
  The error begins with `giong needs io_uring, which is not available here`
  ([GIONG-E0001](https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v0.5.0/docs/errors/E0001.md)).
- `Builder::driver(DriverKind::Epoll)`, or `GIONG_DRIVER=epoll`, uses epoll even where
  io_uring is available.

## Check a machine

```sh
uname -r                              # 6.0 or newer
cat /proc/sys/kernel/io_uring_disabled  # Linux 6.6+: 0 = allowed
ulimit -l                             # Linux 6.14-7.2: unlimited, or 150 KiB per worker
```

`kernel.io_uring_disabled` (Linux 6.6 and newer): `0` allows io_uring for every process,
`1` only for privileged processes and members of the group in `kernel.io_uring_group`,
`2` for nobody. Set it with `sysctl -w kernel.io_uring_disabled=0`, or put the service's
user in that group.

## Locked-memory limit

Linux 6.14 to 7.2 count the memory of every io_uring ring against the locked-memory limit
(`RLIMIT_MEMLOCK`, `ulimit -l`) of a process that lacks `CAP_IPC_LOCK`. Linux 7.3 stopped,
and so did 6.18 from 6.18.58; distribution kernels may have taken the change too. The
count is kept per user ID and summed over all of that user's processes, and the memory of
a closed ring is given back a moment after the close. A giong worker locks about 150 KiB
with the default settings: the submission and completion queues take 136 KiB of it
(`Builder::ring_entries`), the two rings of receive buffers 8 KiB each
(`Builder::recv_buffers`). The usual default limit of 8 MiB holds about fifty workers, for
all of the user's processes together; the 64 KiB of older systems holds none.

A worker that cannot lock the memory gets `ENOMEM` from the kernel, which giong reports as
[GIONG-E0010](https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v0.5.0/docs/errors/E0010.md), naming the limit; without an explicit driver it runs that
worker on epoll and says so once on stderr. Root is not held to the limit, since it has
`CAP_IPC_LOCK`, except where that capability was taken away, as in a Docker container.
Raise the limit, or lift it, for any service that is not root:

- systemd: `LimitMEMLOCK=infinity` in the `[Service]` section, or
  `AmbientCapabilities=CAP_IPC_LOCK` to lift it for a service with a `User=`.
- Docker: `docker run --ulimit memlock=-1:-1`, or in Docker Compose:

  ```yaml
  services:
    api:
      ulimits:
        memlock:
          soft: -1
          hard: -1
  ```

- Kubernetes has no setting for the limit. Add the capability where the pod's security
  policy allows it (`securityContext.capabilities.add: ["IPC_LOCK"]`; Pod Security's
  `baseline` and `restricted` levels do not), or raise the limit the container runtime
  starts containers with on each node (for containerd, `LimitMEMLOCK=infinity` in a
  drop-in for its systemd unit). Containers that run as the same user ID on one node share
  the count.
- A shell: `ulimit -l unlimited` as root before starting the service, or an entry in
  `/etc/security/limits.conf` for its user.

Or need less: fewer workers, a smaller `Builder::ring_entries`, fewer receive buffers. Or
run a kernel that does not count the rings.

## Ubuntu 24.04

Ubuntu's 6.8 kernels from 6.8.0-135 on have a bug that makes them refuse every correctly
formed io_uring buffer ring, which giong's io_uring driver needs: a backport inverted a
check on the request's reserved fields. The AWS, Azure, GCP and Oracle 6.8 kernels built
from them have it too, as does the 6.8 HWE kernel of Ubuntu 22.04. giong recognises the bug and registers its ring
the way those kernels accept, so io_uring works there at full speed, and
`giong::driver_choice()` lists the workaround (`buffer-ring-reserved-check`). Nothing to
do on your side. Other software that uses buffer rings through liburing fails on those
kernels with `EINVAL`. The 7.0 HWE kernel (`linux-generic-hwe-24.04`) does not have the
bug.

## Docker

Docker's default seccomp profile does not allow the io_uring system calls, so in a
container run with default settings giong uses its epoll driver. For io_uring, use a
profile that is Docker's default plus those three calls:

```sh
curl -fsSLo docker-default.json \
  https://raw.githubusercontent.com/moby/profiles/main/seccomp/default.json
jq '.syscalls += [{"names": ["io_uring_setup", "io_uring_enter", "io_uring_register"],
                   "action": "SCMP_ACT_ALLOW"}]' docker-default.json > giong-seccomp.json

docker run --security-opt seccomp=giong-seccomp.json your-image
```

With Docker Compose:

```yaml
services:
  api:
    image: your-image
    security_opt:
      - seccomp=giong-seccomp.json
```

This keeps every other restriction of the default profile. Avoid
`--security-opt seccomp=unconfined`, which turns all of them off.

Checked on Docker Engine 29.9.2 with a static binary that starts a runtime and does a TCP
round trip: with `giong-seccomp.json` it runs on io_uring. With the default profile,
giong's test suite runs on the epoll driver in CI (the `docker` job).

## Kubernetes

A pod's containers get the container runtime's default profile when their
`securityContext.seccompProfile.type` is `RuntimeDefault`, and also by default on
kubelets started with `--seccomp-default`. Pod Security's `restricted` level requires
either `RuntimeDefault` or `Localhost`. containerd's default profile blocks io_uring like Docker's does.

Install `giong-seccomp.json` from above on every node, under the kubelet's seccomp
directory (by default `/var/lib/kubelet/seccomp/`), for example as
`profiles/giong.json`, and point the container at it:

```yaml
securityContext:
  seccompProfile:
    type: Localhost
    localhostProfile: profiles/giong.json
```

The [Security Profiles Operator](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/security-profiles-operator)
can distribute the profile to the nodes for you. Managed platforms differ in what they
let you change; check that yours allows `Localhost` profiles.

## Sandboxes

Runtimes that put a user-space kernel between the container and Linux, such as gVisor
(used by GKE Sandbox), do not offer io_uring by default. giong runs on epoll there; run it
outside such a sandbox for io_uring.

---

<!-- https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v0.5.0/docs/errors/README.md -->

# Error codes

Every error giong raises itself starts with a code and ends with a link to its page here:

```text
GIONG-E0102: no address found for db.internal. Fix: check the spelling of the name,
/etc/hosts, and the DNS servers in /etc/resolv.conf (in a container, the network it is
attached to). See https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/main/docs/errors/E0102.md
```

Errors giong only passes on, such as "connection refused" from the kernel, have no code.
Functions still return `std::io::Error`; match on the code, not on the message:

```rust
use giong::error::{self, Code};

fn on_error(err: &std::io::Error) {
    if error::code(err) == Some(Code::HostNotFound) {
        // ...
    }
}
```

giong-http, giong-web, giong-tls, giong-postgres, giong-mysql, giong-redis, giong-mcp and
giong-compat use the same codes. A code is never reused or renumbered, and its page stays
when it is no longer raised.

## The runtime

| Code | `Code::` | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| [GIONG-E0001](https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v0.5.0/docs/errors/E0001.md) | `IoUringUnavailable` | io_uring is not available |

<!-- https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v0.5.0/docs/errors/E0001.md -->

# GIONG-E0001: io_uring is not available

Raised by the runtime, when a worker starts. In code: `giong::error::Code::IoUringUnavailable`.

## What happened

The runtime was told to use io_uring (`Builder::driver(DriverKind::IoUring)`, or `GIONG_DRIVER=io_uring`), and `io_uring_setup` failed with `EPERM`, `EACCES` or `ENOSYS`. The kernel has io_uring but this process may not use it, or the kernel (or a sandbox in front of it) does not have it at all. Without that instruction giong would have used its epoll driver instead. The error keeps the kernel's `io::ErrorKind` (`PermissionDenied` or `Unsupported`), and the kernel's error is its `source()`.

## How to fix it

- If epoll is good enough here, stop asking for io_uring: remove `.driver(DriverKind::IoUring)` and unset `GIONG_DRIVER`, and giong falls back to epoll by itself.
- In Docker, the default seccomp profile blocks io_uring. Run with a profile that allows `io_uring_setup`, `io_uring_enter` and `io_uring_register` (see [DEPLOYMENT.md](https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v0.5.0/docs/DEPLOYMENT.md)), or `--security-opt seccomp=unconfined` to confirm that this is the cause.
- In Kubernetes, the container runtime applies the same default profile: set a `seccompProfile` of type `Localhost` that allows the three calls, as [DEPLOYMENT.md](https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v0.5.0/docs/DEPLOYMENT.md) shows.
- On the host, `sysctl kernel.io_uring_disabled` must be `0`, or `1` with the process in the group named by `kernel.io_uring_group`.
- gVisor and some other sandboxes do not offer io_uring by default; run giong outside them.

[All error codes](https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v0.5.0/docs/errors/README.md)

---

<!-- https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v0.5.0/docs/errors/E0002.md -->

# GIONG-E0002: the kernel is too old

Raised by the runtime, when a worker starts. In code: `giong::error::Code::KernelTooOld`.

## What happened

The runtime was told to use io_uring (`Builder::driver(DriverKind::IoUring)`, or `GIONG_DRIVER=io_uring`), and the kernel is missing an io_uring feature giong needs: registering a ring of receive buffers (`IORING_REGISTER_PBUF_RING`) failed. It arrived in Linux 5.19 and works reliably from 6.0, the oldest kernel giong's io_uring driver supports. Without that instruction giong would have used its epoll driver, which works on older kernels.

## How to fix it

- If epoll is good enough here, stop asking for io_uring: remove `.driver(DriverKind::IoUring)` and unset `GIONG_DRIVER`.
- Run on Linux 6.0 or newer; 6.1 or newer is faster (giong then uses `IORING_SETUP_DEFER_TASKRUN`). `uname -r` shows the version.
- On a managed platform, pick a node image with a newer kernel.

[All error codes](https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v0.5.0/docs/errors/README.md)

---

<!-- https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v0.5.0/docs/errors/E0003.md -->

# GIONG-E0003: another runtime handles the signals

Raised by the runtime, when it starts. In code: `giong::error::Code::SignalsTaken`.

## What happened

The runtime was built with `Builder::shutdown_on_signals(true)`, but another giong runtime in this process already handles `SIGINT` and `SIGTERM`. Signal handlers belong to the whole process, so only one runtime at a time can own them.

## How to fix it

- Turn on `shutdown_on_signals` for one runtime only, and stop the others through their `Handle::shutdown`.
- Or run one runtime at a time: the handlers are released when that runtime's `run` returns.

[All error codes](https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v0.5.0/docs/errors/README.md)

---

<!-- https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v0.5.0/docs/errors/E0004.md -->

# GIONG-E0004: invalid runtime setting

Raised by the runtime, when it starts. In code: `giong::error::Code::InvalidConfig`.

## What happened

A runtime setting is outside the range giong accepts, such as the number or the size of the receive buffers, or the `GIONG_DRIVER` environment variable names no driver.

## How to fix it

- Read the message: it names the setting, the range and the value given.
- `Builder::recv_buffers(count, size)` takes up to 32768 buffers, rounded up to a power of two, and a size from 64 bytes to 4 GiB.
- `GIONG_DRIVER` takes `io_uring` or `epoll`; unset or empty (or `auto`) means io_uring where the kernel allows it and epoll elsewhere. It is read only when the code does not call `Builder::driver`.

[All error codes](https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v0.5.0/docs/errors/README.md)

---

<!-- https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v0.5.0/docs/errors/E0005.md -->

# GIONG-E0005: unexpected result from the kernel

Raised by the runtime's I/O operations. In code: `giong::error::Code::Unexpected`.

## What happened

The kernel returned something giong does not expect, such as received data without a buffer or a datagram from an unknown address family. It points to a bug in giong or in the kernel.

## How to fix it

- Please report it at https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/issues with the message, your kernel version (`uname -r`) and, if you can, a way to reproduce it.
- Running the same program on another kernel version helps tell the two apart.

[All error codes](https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v0.5.0/docs/errors/README.md)

---

<!-- https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v0.5.0/docs/errors/E0006.md -->

# GIONG-E0006: read used after recv

Raised by `TcpStream`, `UnixStream` and `UdpSocket`. In code: `giong::error::Code::MixedReads`.

## What happened

A one-off read (`read`, `read_from`) was used on a stream or socket that already has a multishot receive (`recv`, `recv_from`) running. The kernel keeps delivering data into the multishot receive, so a one-off read would see the data out of order.

## How to fix it

- Use one way of reading per stream or socket: `recv`/`recv_from` (buffers from the runtime's pool, best for many connections) or `read`/`read_from` (your own buffer).

[All error codes](https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v0.5.0/docs/errors/README.md)

---

<!-- https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v0.5.0/docs/errors/E0007.md -->

# GIONG-E0007: the time limit passed

Raised by `giong::time::timeout`, when its error becomes an `io::Error`. In code: `giong::error::Code::TimedOut`.

## What happened

The future given to `giong::time::timeout` did not finish within its time limit, and the `Elapsed` error was turned into an `io::Error` (by `?` in a function returning `io::Result`). The future was dropped, which cancels its I/O.

## How to fix it

- Give it more time if the limit is too tight for the work.
- Otherwise find out why the operation is slow: the peer, the network, or a task that keeps the worker busy (one worker runs every task on its core).

[All error codes](https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v0.5.0/docs/errors/README.md)

---

<!-- https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v0.5.0/docs/errors/E0008.md -->

# GIONG-E0008: no such worker

Raised by `giong::Handle::spawn_on`, as a panic. In code: `giong::error::Code::NoSuchWorker`.

## What happened

`spawn_on` was given a worker index that the runtime does not have. Workers are numbered from 0 to `Handle::workers() - 1`. This is a bug in the calling code, so `spawn_on` panics instead of returning an error.

## How to fix it

- Pass an index below `Handle::workers()`. To spread work over every worker, use `i % handle.workers()`.
- `Builder::workers` sets the count; without it, the runtime starts one worker for each CPU the process may run on, which differs between machines and containers.

[All error codes](https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v0.5.0/docs/errors/README.md)

---

<!-- https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v0.5.0/docs/errors/E0009.md -->

# GIONG-E0009: the kernel refused io_uring buffer rings

Raised by the runtime, when a worker starts. In code: `giong::error::Code::BufferRingRefused`.

## What happened

The runtime was told to use io_uring (`Builder::driver(DriverKind::IoUring)`, or `GIONG_DRIVER=io_uring`), the kernel is 6.0 or newer, and it would not register giong's ring of receive buffers (`IORING_REGISTER_PBUF_RING`). Such a kernel should accept it, and giong already works around the kernel bugs it knows here, such as the inverted check in Ubuntu's 6.8.0-135 and later kernels (`giong::KernelWorkaround`). The message names the kernel release, the kernel's error is the `source()`, and its `io::ErrorKind` is kept. Without that instruction giong would have used its epoll driver.

## How to fix it

- If epoll is good enough here, stop asking for io_uring: remove `.driver(DriverKind::IoUring)` and unset `GIONG_DRIVER`. `giong::driver_choice()` then reports this same error as the reason giong chose epoll.
- `ENOMEM` means the memory for the ring could not be had: check the service's memory cgroup limit, or give it fewer receive buffers (`Builder::recv_buffers`). When the locked-memory limit is the cause (Linux 6.14 to 7.2 count buffer rings against it), giong raises [GIONG-E0010](https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v0.5.0/docs/errors/E0010.md) instead.
- `EINVAL` on a 6.x kernel is most likely a kernel bug giong does not know yet. Please report it with the output of `uname -r` at <https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/issues>; a newer kernel of the same distribution may already have it fixed.

[All error codes](https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v0.5.0/docs/errors/README.md)

---

<!-- https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v0.5.0/docs/errors/E0010.md -->

# GIONG-E0010: the locked-memory limit is used up

Raised by the runtime, when a worker starts. In code: `giong::error::Code::LockedMemoryLimit`.

## What happened

Setting up the worker's io_uring failed with `ENOMEM`, and the process is held to a locked-memory limit (`RLIMIT_MEMLOCK`, `ulimit -l`): it is not unlimited, and the process lacks `CAP_IPC_LOCK`, which would lift it. Linux 6.14 to 7.2 count the memory of every io_uring ring against that limit: the submission and completion queues, and each buffer ring (7.3 stopped, and so did 6.18 from 6.18.58). The count is kept per user ID, summed over all of that user's processes, and the kernel gives the memory of a closed ring back a moment after the close, not at once. A giong worker locks about 150 KiB with the default settings, so a limit of 8 MiB, a common default, holds about fifty workers, and one of 64 KiB, the default on older systems, holds none. The message names the limit and what the memory was for ("rings" or "buffer ring"); the kernel's error is the `source()`, and its `io::ErrorKind` (`OutOfMemory`) is kept.

Without `Builder::driver(DriverKind::IoUring)` or `GIONG_DRIVER=io_uring`, giong runs such a worker on its epoll driver instead, says so once on stderr, and `giong::driver_choice()` reports this error as the reason. Workers that got their rings before the limit was used up stay on io_uring.

## How to fix it

- Raise the limit for the service: `LimitMEMLOCK=infinity` in its systemd unit, `--ulimit memlock=-1` with `docker run` (in Docker Compose, `memlock` under `ulimits` with `soft: -1` and `hard: -1`), or `ulimit -l unlimited` in the shell that starts it. [DEPLOYMENT.md](https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v0.5.0/docs/DEPLOYMENT.md#locked-memory-limit) has the details, Kubernetes included.
- Or give the process `CAP_IPC_LOCK`, which lifts the limit (`AmbientCapabilities=CAP_IPC_LOCK` in a systemd unit, `--cap-add IPC_LOCK` with `docker run`).
- Or need less: fewer workers (`Builder::workers`), smaller rings (`Builder::ring_entries`), fewer receive buffers (`Builder::recv_buffers`). Other processes of the same user ID count too, other containers running as that ID on the same machine included.
- Or run a kernel that does not count io_uring's rings: Linux 7.3 or newer, or 6.18.58 or newer in the 6.18 series.
- If epoll is good enough here, stop asking for io_uring: remove `.driver(DriverKind::IoUring)` and unset `GIONG_DRIVER`.

[All error codes](https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v0.5.0/docs/errors/README.md)

---

<!-- https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v0.5.0/docs/errors/E0100.md -->

# GIONG-E0100: invalid address

Raised by `giong::net`, when an address is given as a string. In code: `giong::error::Code::InvalidAddress`.

## What happened

An address string is not `"host:port"`: the port is missing, is not a number from 0 to 65535, or the string is empty.

## How to fix it

- Write the host and the port: `"localhost:8080"`, `"10.0.0.5:5432"`, `"[::1]:443"` (brackets around an IPv6 address).
- A URL is not an address: take the host and the port out of it first.

[All error codes](https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v0.5.0/docs/errors/README.md)

---

<!-- https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v0.5.0/docs/errors/E0101.md -->

# GIONG-E0101: invalid host name

Raised by `giong::net` name resolution. In code: `giong::error::Code::InvalidHostName`.

## What happened

A host name has characters or a shape that DNS does not allow, so it was refused before any query was sent.

## How to fix it

- A name is labels of letters, digits, `-` and `_`, separated by dots; each label is 1 to 63 characters, the whole name at most 253.
- Spaces, empty labels (`a..b`) and non-ASCII characters are not allowed; an internationalized name must be given in its `xn--` form.

[All error codes](https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v0.5.0/docs/errors/README.md)

---

<!-- https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v0.5.0/docs/errors/E0102.md -->

# GIONG-E0102: host not found

Raised by `giong::net` name resolution (`TcpStream::connect`, `lookup_host`, `Resolver`). In code: `giong::error::Code::HostNotFound`.

## What happened

The name has no address. giong looked in `/etc/hosts`, then asked the DNS servers in `/etc/resolv.conf` (with its `search` domains), and they answered that the name does not exist or has no `A` or `AAAA` record.

## How to fix it

- Check the spelling of the name.
- Check `/etc/hosts` and `/etc/resolv.conf`; in a container, check that it is attached to the network where the name is defined (a Docker Compose service; a Kubernetes Service in another namespace needs the namespace in its name).
- `getent hosts <name>` shows what the system resolver finds, for comparison.

[All error codes](https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v0.5.0/docs/errors/README.md)

---

<!-- https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v0.5.0/docs/errors/E0103.md -->

# GIONG-E0103: no address to use

Raised by `giong::net` connect and bind. In code: `giong::error::Code::NoAddresses`.

## What happened

A connect or bind was given an empty list of addresses, so there was nothing to try.

## How to fix it

- Pass at least one address, or a name that resolves to one.

[All error codes](https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v0.5.0/docs/errors/README.md)

---

<!-- https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v0.5.0/docs/errors/E0104.md -->

# GIONG-E0104: no DNS server configured

Raised by `giong::net` name resolution. In code: `giong::error::Code::NoDnsServer`.

## What happened

A name had to be looked up in DNS, but `/etc/resolv.conf` names no DNS server (it is missing, empty, or has no `nameserver` line).

## How to fix it

- Add a `nameserver` line to `/etc/resolv.conf`.
- Or use an IP address, or a name listed in `/etc/hosts`, which need no DNS.

[All error codes](https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v0.5.0/docs/errors/README.md)

---

<!-- https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v0.5.0/docs/errors/E0105.md -->

# GIONG-E0105: DNS server did not answer

Raised by `giong::net` name resolution. In code: `giong::error::Code::DnsTimeout`.

## What happened

No DNS server answered in time, after trying each server in `/etc/resolv.conf` the configured number of times.

## How to fix it

- Check that the servers are reachable from here: a firewall, a VPN or a container network can drop DNS traffic (UDP and TCP port 53).
- `options timeout:N attempts:N` in `/etc/resolv.conf` (or `ResolverConfig::timeout` and `attempts`) give the servers longer.

[All error codes](https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v0.5.0/docs/errors/README.md)

---

<!-- https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v0.5.0/docs/errors/E0106.md -->

# GIONG-E0106: DNS server failed

Raised by `giong::net` name resolution. In code: `giong::error::Code::DnsServerFailure`.

## What happened

A DNS server answered, but with an error such as `SERVFAIL` (it could not get an answer from upstream) or `REFUSED` (it will not answer this client). That is different from the name not existing (`GIONG-E0102`).

## How to fix it

- Try again: `SERVFAIL` is often temporary.
- Check the DNS server: its logs, and whether it allows queries from this machine.
- If the name is in a private zone, check that this server is the one that serves it.

[All error codes](https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v0.5.0/docs/errors/README.md)

---

<!-- https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v0.5.0/docs/errors/E0107.md -->

# GIONG-E0107: malformed DNS answer

Raised by `giong::net` name resolution. In code: `giong::error::Code::DnsBadResponse`.

## What happened

A DNS server sent an answer giong cannot read, or closed a TCP connection before answering. Something between giong and the server may be changing or cutting the traffic.

## How to fix it

- Check the DNS server named in the message.
- Check for middleboxes that rewrite DNS or block TCP on port 53 (large answers are fetched over TCP).
- If the server is standard and the answer looks valid to `dig`, please report it at https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/issues.

[All error codes](https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v0.5.0/docs/errors/README.md)

---

<!-- https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v0.5.0/docs/errors/E0200.md -->

# GIONG-E0200: invalid path

Raised by `giong::fs`. In code: `giong::error::Code::InvalidPath`.

## What happened

A path contains a NUL byte. Linux paths are passed to the kernel as C strings, which end at the first NUL, so such a path cannot name any file.

## How to fix it

- Remove the NUL byte; it usually comes from unchecked input or a fixed-size buffer converted whole.

[All error codes](https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v0.5.0/docs/errors/README.md)

---

<!-- https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v0.5.0/docs/errors/E0201.md -->

# GIONG-E0201: the file ended before the bytes to send

Raised by `giong::net::TcpStream::send_file`, and by the `send_file` of `giong-tls` and `giong-http` built on it. In code: `giong::error::Code::FileTooShort`.

## What happened

`send_file` was asked to send `len` bytes from `offset`, and the file ends before `offset + len`. The bytes the file had were sent; the peer received fewer than it was told to expect. This usually means the file was truncated or replaced between the moment its size was read and the moment it was sent, or the range was computed from the wrong file.

The connection is not closed, but whatever announced the length (an HTTP `Content-Length`, a length prefix) is now wrong, so the peer will wait for bytes that never come. Close the connection.

## How to fix it

- Take the length from the open file itself (`File::len`), not from a separate `metadata` call on the path, so that both describe the same file.
- If the file can change while it is served, write the new version to a temporary file and `rename` it over the old one: an open file keeps its old contents.
- Check `offset + len <= file.len()?` before calling `send_file` when the range comes from a request (an HTTP `Range` header).

[All error codes](https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v0.5.0/docs/errors/README.md)

---

<!-- https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v0.5.0/docs/errors/E1101.md -->

# GIONG-E1101: invalid HTTP request

Raised by giong-http's client, before anything is sent. In code: `giong::error::Code::HttpClientRequest`.

## What happened

The request could not be sent as written: the URL is not an absolute `http` or `https` URL, a header name or value is not valid, the method is not a token, or a header that frames the message was set by hand. The message names the part. Nothing was sent.

## How to fix it

- Write the URL whole: `https://host[:port]/path?query`. Percent-encode spaces and other bytes that are not visible ASCII (`%20` for a space); give a non-ASCII host name in its `xn--` form.
- User names and passwords in the URL are not sent: set an `Authorization` header instead.
- `Content-Length`, `Transfer-Encoding`, `Connection`, `Upgrade` and `TE` are set by the client from the body and the connection; leave them out.
- A header value cannot contain a line break: that would let it start a header of its own.

[All error codes](https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v0.5.0/docs/errors/README.md)

---

<!-- https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v0.5.0/docs/errors/E1102.md -->

# GIONG-E1102: cannot connect to the HTTP server

Raised by giong-http's client, opening a connection. In code: `giong::error::Code::HttpClientConnect`.

## What happened

Opening the connection failed: the host name did not resolve, the TCP connection was refused or did not answer, the TLS handshake failed (the certificate was not valid for the host, or not issued by a trusted authority), or it all took longer than the connect timeout (10 seconds by default). The cause is in the message, with the code of the network or TLS error that caused it.

## How to fix it

- Check the host and the port, and that the server is reachable from here (`curl -v` from the same machine or container shows the same thing).
- For certificate errors, see the TLS code in the message (`GIONG-E2004`): the certificate must name the host in the URL. A private authority is trusted with `ClientBuilder::tls(TlsConnector::with_root_pem(..))`.
- On a machine without certificate authorities installed (a `FROM scratch` image), install `ca-certificates` or pass `TlsConnector::with_webpki_roots()` (giong-tls's `webpki-roots` feature).
- If the server is far away or slow to accept, raise `ClientBuilder::connect_timeout`.
- Through a proxy, the message names the proxy when it is the proxy that cannot be reached: check its address, or leave the host out with `Proxy::no_proxy`.
- It is transient (`Error::is_transient`): retrying after a pause can work.

[All error codes](https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v0.5.0/docs/errors/README.md)

---

<!-- https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v0.5.0/docs/errors/E1103.md -->

# GIONG-E1103: HTTP request timed out

Raised by giong-http's client, any request. In code: `giong::error::Code::HttpClientTimeout`.

## What happened

The request did not finish within its timeout (30 seconds by default). The timeout covers the whole request: waiting for a free connection, connecting, sending, reading the whole response, and following redirects. The request was dropped, and the connection it used was closed.

## How to fix it

- If the server is known to be slow, raise the timeout for that request (`RequestBuilder::timeout`) or for the client (`ClientBuilder::timeout`).
- If many requests wait for a connection to the same host, raise `ClientBuilder::max_connections_per_host` (16 by default).
- Otherwise find out why the server is slow; the error is transient, but a retry adds load to a server that is already behind.

[All error codes](https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v0.5.0/docs/errors/README.md)

---

<!-- https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v0.5.0/docs/errors/E1104.md -->

# GIONG-E1104: HTTP response too large

Raised by giong-http's client, reading a response. In code: `giong::error::Code::HttpClientTooLarge`.

## What happened

The response was larger than the client accepts: its body over `ClientBuilder::max_response_size` (16 MiB by default), or its head (status line and headers) over `ClientBuilder::max_head_size` (64 KiB). The connection was closed rather than read to the end.

## How to fix it

- If such responses are expected, raise the limit on the client that fetches them.
- For an API that can return very large results, ask for less at a time (pagination, a narrower query).

[All error codes](https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v0.5.0/docs/errors/README.md)

---

<!-- https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v0.5.0/docs/errors/E1105.md -->

# GIONG-E1105: redirect not followed

Raised by giong-http's client, following redirects. In code: `giong::error::Code::HttpClientRedirect`.

## What happened

A redirect was not followed: there were more than `ClientBuilder::redirects` of them (10 by default), it pointed from an `https` URL to an `http` one, or its `Location` was not a valid URL. The message has the redirect's target.

## How to fix it

- A redirect loop is a server problem; the message shows where it pointed last.
- A redirect from HTTPS to HTTP would send the request, and its credentials, in clear text: fix the server, or request the `http` URL directly if that is really wanted.
- To handle redirects yourself, build the client with `redirects(0)`: 3xx responses are then returned as they are.

[All error codes](https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v0.5.0/docs/errors/README.md)

---

<!-- https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v0.5.0/docs/errors/E1106.md -->

# GIONG-E1106: connection closed before the response

Raised by giong-http's client, sending a request or reading a response. In code: `giong::error::Code::HttpClientClosed`.

## What happened

The connection closed, or failed, before the whole response arrived. On a connection that had carried requests before, this usually means the server closed it as the request was sent; an idempotent request (GET, HEAD, PUT, DELETE, OPTIONS) is then sent once more on a new connection by itself, so this error means that failed too, or that the request was a POST or PATCH, which the server may have processed.

Over HTTP/2 the same error covers a stream the server reset (`RST_STREAM`; the message names its error code, such as `INTERNAL_ERROR` or `CANCEL`) and a connection the server closed with GOAWAY. A request the server says it did not process (`REFUSED_STREAM`, or a stream beyond the last one a GOAWAY names) is sent again by itself, whatever its method, up to five times in a row.

## How to fix it

- Retry if the request is safe to repeat (`Error::is_transient` is true).
- If it happens often on idle connections, lower `ClientBuilder::idle_timeout` below the server's (or its load balancer's) keep-alive timeout.
- If it happens in the middle of a response, look at the server's logs: it may have crashed or hit its own limit.
- If the message says the server closed the connection **without a TLS close_notify**: the response had no length and was meant to end where the connection ends, but over HTTPS only a `close_notify` alert proves that the server ended it, so the client refuses a body that may have been cut short by someone on the network path (a truncation attack). Make the server send `Content-Length` or chunked responses, or close its TLS connections properly.

[All error codes](https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v0.5.0/docs/errors/README.md)

---

<!-- https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v0.5.0/docs/errors/E1107.md -->

# GIONG-E1107: malformed HTTP response

Raised by giong-http's client, reading a response. In code: `giong::error::Code::HttpClientProtocol`.

## What happened

The server sent something that is not a valid HTTP/1.1 response, or one this client refuses because it could be read in two ways: two different `Content-Length` headers, lines that end in a bare line feed, folded header lines, a malformed chunked body, a `Transfer-Encoding` other than chunked (such as gzip), or a switch to another protocol. The connection was closed and is not used again.

Over HTTP/2 the server broke a rule of RFC 9113 instead. On one stream (a response head with an uppercase or connection-specific field such as `connection`, no `:status`, a body longer or shorter than its `content-length`, more data than the stream's flow-control window allowed), the stream is reset and the connection goes on carrying the other requests. On the whole connection (a frame that is malformed or out of place, a header block that does not decode, more data than the connection's window allowed, `SETTINGS_ENABLE_PUSH` or a `PUSH_PROMISE` from the server), the client sends a GOAWAY and every request on the connection fails.

## How to fix it

- Check that the URL points at an HTTP server, on the right port and scheme (`https` for a TLS port).
- A proxy or server sending ambiguous framing is a bug there; the message says which rule was broken.
- `Transfer-Encoding: gzip` is not read (the client decompresses `Content-Encoding: gzip` and `deflate` only): make the server use `Content-Encoding`.
- Over HTTP/2, the message names the rule. A server that gets HTTP/2 wrong can be spoken to over HTTP/1.1 with `ClientBuilder::http2(false)` until it is fixed.

[All error codes](https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v0.5.0/docs/errors/README.md)

---

<!-- https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v0.5.0/docs/errors/E1108.md -->

# GIONG-E1108: HTTP error status

Raised by giong-http's client, `Response::error_for_status`. In code: `giong::error::Code::HttpClientStatus`.

## What happened

The response has a 4xx (client error) or 5xx (server error) status, and the program asked for that to be an error. The message has the status and the start of the body, where APIs usually say what was wrong; `Error::status` has the code.

## How to fix it

- Read the body in the message: for 400 and 422 it usually names the field that was refused.
- 401 and 403: check the credentials and their scope.
- 429, 502, 503 and 504 are transient (`Error::is_transient`): retry after a pause, honouring the `Retry-After` header if the response has one.

[All error codes](https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v0.5.0/docs/errors/README.md)

---

<!-- https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v0.5.0/docs/errors/E1109.md -->

# GIONG-E1109: cannot decode the response body

Raised by giong-http's client, reading a body. In code: `giong::error::Code::HttpClientDecode`.

## What happened

The body could not be read the way it was asked for: `Response::text` found bytes that are not UTF-8, or a body the server compressed (`Content-Encoding: gzip` or `deflate`) could not be decompressed: the compressed data is damaged, fails its checksum, or ends before it should (a response cut short).

## How to fix it

- For text: read it as bytes with `Response::body`, and decode it with the character set its `Content-Type` names.
- For a compressed body: the server sent damaged data, or the connection was cut. Retrying can help if it was cut. To see the bytes as they came, send the request with its own `Accept-Encoding` header, or build the client with `ClientBuilder::decompress(false)`.
- Encodings the client does not decode (`br`, `zstd`) are never an error: the body comes as it was sent, with its `Content-Encoding` header.

[All error codes](https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v0.5.0/docs/errors/README.md)

---

<!-- https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v0.5.0/docs/errors/E1110.md -->

# GIONG-E1110: the HTTP proxy refused the request

Raised by giong-http's client, through a proxy. In code: `giong::error::Code::HttpClientProxy`.

## What happened

The proxy given with `ClientBuilder::proxy` (or read by `Proxy::from_env`) would not open a tunnel to an `https` server: it asked for credentials (407), its rules do not allow the host or port (403), it could not reach the server (502, 504), or it answered with something that is not HTTP. `Error::status` has the proxy's status, if it sent one. A proxy that cannot be reached at all is `GIONG-E1102` instead. For an `http` URL the proxy's answer, 407 included, is the response.

## How to fix it

- 407: put the user name and password in the proxy's URL, `http://user:password@proxy:3128` (with `%40` for an `@` in either). They are sent only to the proxy, never to the server.
- 403: the proxy's own rules refuse the destination. If the host should be reached without the proxy (a service in the same cluster, say), add it to `Proxy::no_proxy` or `NO_PROXY`: `.svc.cluster.local, 10.0.0.0/8`.
- 502 or 504: the proxy could not reach the server; this one is transient (`Error::is_transient`). Check the host from the proxy's side.
- An answer that is not HTTP: the proxy URL points at something else (a SOCKS proxy, or the wrong port). Only `http://` proxies are supported.

[All error codes](https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v0.5.0/docs/errors/README.md)

---

<!-- https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v0.5.0/docs/errors/E1111.md -->

# GIONG-E1111: request body too large

Raised by giong-http's server, to a handler reading a request body as a stream. In code: `giong::error::Code::HttpBodyTooLarge`.

## What happened

The handler's `Handler::stream_body` returned `Some(limit)`, and the body grew past `limit` bytes. A body that announces a longer `Content-Length` never gets this far: the server answers `413 Content Too Large` without calling the handler. So this is a chunked body, whose length is not known in advance, or a limit passed to `BodyStream::read_to_end`. The connection closes after the response, since the rest of the body is not read.

## How to fix it

- Answer `413 Content Too Large`. In giong-web, `?` on the error does that.
- If bodies this large are expected, raise the limit `stream_body` returns (or `Router::stream_bodies` in giong-web), or the one given to `read_to_end`.

[All error codes](https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v0.5.0/docs/errors/README.md)

---

<!-- https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v0.5.0/docs/errors/E1112.md -->

# GIONG-E1112: request body cut short

Raised by giong-http's server, to a handler reading a request body as a stream. In code: `giong::error::Code::HttpBodyIncomplete`.

## What happened

The body ended before its end. Either the client closed the connection, cancelled the request (an HTTP/2 client resets its stream with `RST_STREAM`) or sent nothing for the server's `request_timeout` (each piece of a streamed body gets that long, counted from the one before; the whole body has no deadline), or the handler had already returned its response, so the connection stopped reading the body. The second happens to a `BodyStream` kept past the response, in a task of its own for example.

## How to fix it

- A client that went away or stalled: nothing to fix on the server. The client may retry. For clients on slow links, raise `Server::request_timeout`.
- A stream read after the response: read the body to its end before returning the response, or stop reading it once the response is returned.

[All error codes](https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v0.5.0/docs/errors/README.md)

---

<!-- https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v0.5.0/docs/errors/E1113.md -->

# GIONG-E1113: malformed request body

Raised by giong-http's server, to a handler reading a request body as a stream. In code: `giong::error::Code::HttpBodyMalformed`.

## What happened

The request body uses `Transfer-Encoding: chunked`, and its framing is broken: a chunk size that is not hexadecimal, a chunk not followed by CRLF, a line longer than 4 KiB, or more than 16 KiB of chunk extensions in all. The pieces before the broken framing were delivered. The connection closes after the response.

Over HTTP/2 the client broke a rule of the request's stream instead: a body longer or shorter than its `content-length`, or more data than the flow-control window allowed. The server resets the stream (`RST_STREAM`); the connection goes on.

## How to fix it

- Answer `400 Bad Request`. In giong-web, `?` on the error does that.
- The client (or a proxy in between) sent an invalid body. Check what it sends with `curl -v` or a packet capture.

[All error codes](https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v0.5.0/docs/errors/README.md)

---

<!-- https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v0.5.0/docs/errors/E1114.md -->

# GIONG-E1114: response body not sent

Raised by giong-http's server, to the code producing a streamed response body. In code: `giong::error::Code::HttpBodyNotSent`.

## What happened

`BodySender::send` was called, but nothing more of the body will reach the client: the client went away (closed the connection, or did not read for the server's `write_timeout`), or the response never had a body to send (an answer to `HEAD`, or status 204 or 304), so the server dropped it. A client that goes away is noticed at the next write.

## How to fix it

- Stop producing the body. Nothing is wrong on the server; this is how a producer learns that its client is gone.
- An event stream (`text/event-stream`) that is quiet for long stretches can send a comment line (`: keep-alive`) every 15 to 30 seconds, so a client that went away is noticed then instead of at the next event.

[All error codes](https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v0.5.0/docs/errors/README.md)

---

<!-- https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v0.5.0/docs/errors/E1115.md -->

# GIONG-E1115: HTTP/2 protocol error

Sent by giong-http's server to an HTTP/2 client, in the debug data of the GOAWAY frame that closes the connection. In code: `giong::error::Code::Http2Protocol`.

## What happened

The client broke a rule of HTTP/2 (RFC 9113) that leaves the whole connection in doubt, so the server closed it. The GOAWAY carries the error code the RFC asks for (`PROTOCOL_ERROR`, `FRAME_SIZE_ERROR`, `FLOW_CONTROL_ERROR`, `COMPRESSION_ERROR` or `STREAM_CLOSED`) and, after this code, the rule that was broken, for example:

```text
GIONG-E1115: DATA on a stream that was never opened
GIONG-E1115: a header block was interrupted by another frame
GIONG-E1115: the connection did not start with the HTTP/2 preface
```

Requests already being answered are cut off. A mistake that only concerns one stream (a malformed request, a body longer than its `content-length`) resets that stream instead, and the connection goes on.

## How to fix it

- The client, or a proxy in between, has a bug. Read the rule in the debug data, then look at the frames it sends: `nghttp -nv https://host/` or `curl -v --http2` for a request of your own, a packet capture with TLS keys (`SSLKEYLOGFILE`) otherwise.
- A client that speaks HTTP/1.1 to a port where it should speak HTTP/2, or the other way round, is answered as HTTP/1.1 on a plain port and through ALPN over TLS, so it should not land here. Over plain TCP, HTTP/2 needs prior knowledge (`curl --http2-prior-knowledge`); the `Upgrade: h2c` handshake is not supported.

[All error codes](https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v0.5.0/docs/errors/README.md)

---

<!-- https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v0.5.0/docs/errors/E1116.md -->

# GIONG-E1116: too many HTTP/2 streams reset

Sent by giong-http's server to an HTTP/2 client, in the debug data of the GOAWAY frame (`ENHANCE_YOUR_CALM`) that closes the connection. In code: `giong::error::Code::Http2TooManyResets`.

## What happened

The client cancelled (`RST_STREAM`) more streams before their answer than the server allows in a short time, or had that many refused or reset by the server. Opening a stream and cancelling it at once makes the server start work that nobody waits for; done in a loop, this is the "rapid reset" attack (CVE-2023-44487). The server allows a burst of twice `max_concurrent_streams` (at least 100) and then `max_concurrent_streams` per second (at least 50).

The server also drops the handler of a cancelled stream at once, so a cancelled request costs little; the limit keeps the cost per connection bounded.

## How to fix it

- If the client is yours: cancel fewer requests, or open new streams more slowly after cancelling. Browsers and well-known HTTP/2 libraries stay far below the limit.
- A client that keeps opening streams beyond `SETTINGS_MAX_CONCURRENT_STREAMS` has them refused, which counts too: make it respect the limit the server announces (`Server::max_concurrent_streams`, default 100).
- Otherwise the client is misbehaving or attacking, and closing the connection is the intended outcome.

[All error codes](https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v0.5.0/docs/errors/README.md)

---

<!-- https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v0.5.0/docs/errors/E1117.md -->

# GIONG-E1117: too many HTTP/2 control frames

Sent by giong-http's server to an HTTP/2 client, in the debug data of the GOAWAY frame (`ENHANCE_YOUR_CALM`) that closes the connection. In code: `giong::error::Code::Http2Flood`.

## What happened

The client sent more frames that do no work than the server allows in a short time: PING, SETTINGS and their acknowledgements, PRIORITY, empty DATA or CONTINUATION frames, WINDOW_UPDATE frames when nothing waits to be sent, frames for streams already closed, header blocks for streams the server ignores, and frame types the server does not know. Each costs the server some work and buys the client nothing, so a stream of them is a flood (the "ping flood", "settings flood", "empty frames" and CONTINUATION attacks). The server allows a burst of 1,000 such frames and then 500 per second.

## How to fix it

- If the client is yours: send keep-alive PINGs every few seconds at most, and SETTINGS only when something changes. Send WINDOW_UPDATE as data is consumed, not on a timer.
- Otherwise the client is misbehaving or attacking, and closing the connection is the intended outcome.

[All error codes](https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v0.5.0/docs/errors/README.md)

---

<!-- https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v0.5.0/docs/errors/E1118.md -->

# GIONG-E1118: HTTP/2 header block too large

Sent by giong-http's server to an HTTP/2 client, in the debug data of the GOAWAY frame (`ENHANCE_YOUR_CALM`) that closes the connection. In code: `giong::error::Code::Http2HeadersTooLarge`.

## What happened

A header block (a HEADERS frame and the CONTINUATION frames after it) grew past the larger of the server's `max_head_size` and 16 KiB before it ended. The server must keep a block until its end to decode it, so a block that does not end is the CONTINUATION flood. The connection closes, since the HPACK state of the connection depends on the block that was cut off.

A header block within that size whose fields decode to more than `max_head_size` (which the server announces as `SETTINGS_MAX_HEADER_LIST_SIZE`) is not this error: that request gets `431 Request Header Fields Too Large` and the connection goes on.

## How to fix it

- Send smaller headers: large cookies and long custom headers are the usual cause. Or raise `Server::max_head_size` (default 64 KiB) if such headers are expected.
- A client that never ends its header block is misbehaving or attacking, and closing the connection is the intended outcome.

[All error codes](https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v0.5.0/docs/errors/README.md)

---

<!-- https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v0.5.0/docs/errors/E1201.md -->

# GIONG-E1201: invalid route pattern

Raised by giong-web as a panic, when a route is added to a `Router` (`get`, `post`, `route`, `nest`...). The panic points at the line that added it. In code: `giong::error::Code::WebInvalidRoute`.

## What happened

The pattern is not one the router understands. The message quotes the pattern and says what is wrong with it: it does not start with `/`, it has an empty segment (`//`), a segment mixes text and a parameter (`/files/{name}.json`), a parameter name is not letters, digits and `_`, a name appears twice, a catch-all is not the last segment, or a segment has characters that a path cannot hold unencoded. `nest` also refuses a prefix that ends with `/` or with a catch-all.

## How to fix it

- Write each segment as plain text, one parameter `{name}`, or, last, one catch-all `{*name}`: `/users/{id}`, `/files/{*path}`.
- Write text as it is, not percent-encoded: `/café` cannot be a route, `/cafe` can. The router decodes `%XX` in the request's path before comparing.
- To match a file extension, take the whole segment as a parameter (`/files/{name}`) and check the ending in the handler.
- Give nested routers a prefix without a trailing slash: `nest("/api", router)`. The nested router's `/` route then answers `/api`.
- A pattern has at most 16 parameters.

[All error codes](https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v0.5.0/docs/errors/README.md)

---

<!-- https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v0.5.0/docs/errors/E1202.md -->

# GIONG-E1202: route added twice

Raised by giong-web as a panic, when a route is added to a `Router` that already has one with the same method and pattern. In code: `giong::error::Code::WebDuplicateRoute`.

## What happened

Two routes would answer exactly the same requests: same method, and the same pattern once parameter names are left out (`/users/{id}` and `/users/{name}` are the same). The message names both and where the first one was added. It also happens when `nest` brings in a route that the outer router has already.

## How to fix it

- Remove one of the two routes, or give them different paths.
- Different parameter names at the same place do not make different routes: the router cannot tell `{id}` from `{name}` in a path. Use one route and read the parameter as one type, or use different text before it (`/users/by-id/{id}`, `/users/by-name/{name}`).
- Routes that differ only in the method are fine: `get("/users", ...)` and `post("/users", ...)`.

[All error codes](https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v0.5.0/docs/errors/README.md)

---

<!-- https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v0.5.0/docs/errors/E1203.md -->

# GIONG-E1203: no route for the path

Raised by giong-web for a request whose path matches no route: answered with `404 Not Found`. In code: `giong::error::Code::WebNoRoute`.

## What happened

No route's pattern matches the request's path, whatever the method. Paths are matched exactly: a trailing slash makes a different path, case matters, and the query string is not part of the path. When the same path with or without a trailing slash has a route, the detail says so (`did you mean /users?`).

## How to fix it

- For the client: check the path against the service's routes, including the trailing slash and the version prefix (`/api/v1/...`).
- For the service: make sure the route is added to the router that is built and served, with the prefix you expect if it sits in a nested router.

[All error codes](https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v0.5.0/docs/errors/README.md)

---

<!-- https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v0.5.0/docs/errors/E1204.md -->

# GIONG-E1204: method not allowed

Raised by giong-web for a request whose path has routes but none for its method: answered with `405 Method Not Allowed`. In code: `giong::error::Code::WebMethodNotAllowed`.

## What happened

The path matches at least one route, but none of them is for the request's method. The response's `Allow` header lists the methods the path does take; `HEAD` is answered by a `GET` route and `OPTIONS` by the router itself, so they are always listed where they apply.

## How to fix it

- For the client: use one of the methods in `Allow`.
- For the service: add a route for the method, such as `.put("/users/{id}", update)`.

[All error codes](https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v0.5.0/docs/errors/README.md)

---

<!-- https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v0.5.0/docs/errors/E1205.md -->

# GIONG-E1205: invalid path or query parameter

Raised by giong-web's `Req::param`, `Req::query_param` and `Req::query`: answered with `400 Bad Request`. In code: `giong::error::Code::WebBadParameter`.

## What happened

A path or query parameter could not be read as the type the handler asked for, a required query parameter is missing, or the value is not valid percent-encoded UTF-8. The detail names the parameter, quotes the value (cut at 64 characters) and says what was expected, such as ``path parameter `id`: cannot read "abc" (invalid digit found in string); expected an unsigned integer``.

## How to fix it

- For the client: send the parameter in the form the detail asks for. Percent-encode reserved characters in values (`%20` or `+` for a space in a query string, `%2F` for a `/` inside a path parameter).
- For the service: an `Option` field or `query_param` returning `None` makes a parameter optional; use `unwrap_or` for a default. With `Req::query`, a key given twice is an error, and lists are not supported.

[All error codes](https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v0.5.0/docs/errors/README.md)

---

<!-- https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v0.5.0/docs/errors/E1206.md -->

# GIONG-E1206: the route has no such parameter

Raised by giong-web's `Req::param`: answered with `500 Internal Server Error`. The client gets only the code; the server's log has the route and the name. In code: `giong::error::Code::WebNoSuchParameter`.

## What happened

The handler asked for a path parameter that the route which matched does not have: usually a misspelt name (`req.param("idd")` for `/users/{id}`), or a handler shared by several routes that do not all have the parameter. This is a bug in the service, not in the request.

## How to fix it

- Use one of the names in braces in the route's pattern. The log line names the pattern.
- A handler used by several routes can check `req.route()` before asking, or take the value from the query string instead.

[All error codes](https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v0.5.0/docs/errors/README.md)

---

<!-- https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v0.5.0/docs/errors/E1207.md -->

# GIONG-E1207: unreadable request body

Raised by giong-web's `Req::json` (feature `serde`): answered with `400 Bad Request` for a body that is not valid JSON, and `422 Unprocessable Content` for valid JSON of the wrong shape. In code: `giong::error::Code::WebBadBody`.

## What happened
